This chapter introduces the DYNABIC framework, a comprehensive and adaptive cybersecurity solution designed to enhance the resilience of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) in the face of evolving cyber-physical threats. The framework integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, artificial intelligence, and cyber threat intelligence to enable real-time threat detection, simulation, and response. At its core, DYNABIC employs a bidirectionally synchronized digital twin to model and simulate cyber-physical systems, supporting dynamic risk mitigation and adaptive response strategies across the four phases of the resilience cycle: Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, and Adapt. The architecture is modular and scalable, fostering collaboration among CIs and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). It includes key components such as MADT4BC, SOAR4BC, RISKM4BC, SIM4BC, AWARE4BC, and CTI4BC, which collectively support real-time monitoring, risk assessment, incident simulation, automated response, and threat intelligence sharing. The framework also incorporates a human-in-the-loop interface (AVATAR4BC) to enhance situational awareness and decision-making.

This study examines the effect of transformational leadership and employee engagement on employee performance within the service industry. As organizations in this sector increasingly compete on service quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, understanding the human factors that drive employee performance has become a strategic priority for management. Transformational leadership, characterized by idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, is theorized to enhance employees' motivation, commitment, and willingness to exceed expected job requirements. Similarly, employee engagement, reflecting the degree of vigor, dedication, and absorption employees exhibit toward their work, is considered a critical psychological state that translates leadership influence into tangible performance outcomes. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method distributed to employees working in service-based organizations. Data were collected through structured questionnaires measuring transformational leadership, employee engagement, and employee performance, and were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings reveal that both transformational leadership and employee engagement have a positive and significant effect on employee performance, whether tested partially or simultaneously. Transformational leadership was found to strengthen employees' sense of purpose and trust in their leaders, which in turn fosters higher engagement and, consequently, improved performance outcomes. Employee engagement was also identified as a key mediating mechanism linking leadership behavior to performance results. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on leadership and human resource management by providing empirical evidence from the service industry context, where interpersonal interaction and employee behavior directly affect service delivery quality.

As automated vehicles become more prevalent on public roadways, driver responses to critical takeover events require closer attention. This study examined how ADHD diagnosis, rain, and non-driving-related task engagement affect automated-to-manual takeover transitions. Participants completed conditionally automated drives in a simulated freeway environment that varied according to the presence of rain and distraction. Driving performance, takeover response, physiological workload, and post-drive subjective workload were assessed. Findings indicated that rain and distraction affected takeover performance, workload, speed variability, and steering variability. Results also indicated that drivers with ADHD displayed greater speed and steering variability in the presence of rain and distraction. These results suggest that reduced visibility and NDRT engagement can increase the demands of regaining manual control. Overall, the findings indicate that roadway conditions, attentional demands, and individual differences can influence takeover quality. Implications include safer in-vehicle monitoring systems, improved takeover alert systems, and targeted driver training.

This article examines the historical emergence, stages of development, and significance of upbringing technologies in contemporary pedagogical practice. It analyzes the educational and moral perspectives of Eastern thinkers from ancient times, the gradual improvement of traditional upbringing methods, and the integration of modern pedagogical technologies into educational processes. Particular attention is paid to the future prospects of upbringing technologies, including the application of digital educational tools, interactive methods, and artificial intelligence. Furthermore, the article discusses the pedagogical importance of developing moral and ethical qualities among younger generations, preserving national values, and improving contemporary approaches to upbringing. It emphasizes the need to integrate historical educational traditions with modern innovations to foster the comprehensive personal and social development of students. Keywords: upbringing, upbringing technologies, pedagogical technology, historical development, moral and ethical education, national values

Purpose The purpose of this paper is to examine the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven experiential learning in entrepreneurship education in the digital era and to identify the main research trends, intellectual foundations and future directions shaping the field. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a bibliometric approach using 204 Web of Science-indexed articles and reviews published between 2016 and June 2026. Performance analysis and science mapping were conducted using VOSviewer 1.6.20, including publication trajectory, source performance, co-citation, document citation, author productivity, keyword co-occurrence and overlay analyses. Findings The findings show that the field has shifted from limited early activity to rapid expansion during 2024–2026, driven by growing attention to generative AI, AI literacy and educational technology. Three knowledge bases are identified: educational technology and digital pedagogy; entrepreneurship, business and management education; and sustainability-oriented transformation. Five thematic clusters further highlight behavioural competency, AI integration in higher education, socio-technical adaptation, crisis-driven experiential learning and student-centred instructional design. Originality/value The paper contributes a bibliometric research roadmap for AI-driven experiential entrepreneurship education by identifying the field's intellectual structure, thematic development and future research directions. It positions AI not only as a digital tool, but as part of a wider pedagogical shift toward adaptive, responsible and precarity-aware entrepreneurial learning ecosystems.

Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024–2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the comparative analysis in Section 10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also review evidence on where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, including benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches that can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments run on a MacBook Air M1, which offer only limited, illustrative support for these claims. First, the best model class depends on the data regime: a linear AR/ARMA baseline was best on stationary low-SNR data and across all tested SNR levels in our setup, RLS adapted best under parameter drift, and an LSTM was best only on a high-SNR nonlinear process. Second, a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST. Third, trained autoregressors and MLPs do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks. Fourth, a proposed VECM regularizer keeps forecast spreads stationary in a bivariate cointegrated setup, though it does so by producing spread forecasts with much lower variance than the true spread. All experiments use synthetic data, and validation on real financial series remains future work.

The accelerating development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), data-driven systems and autonomous digital platforms leads to profound transformations in modern e-business. These transformations are increasingly conceptualized through the notion of technological singularity, which is understood not as a singular future event but as an ongoing process of escalating algorithmic autonomy, systemic complexity and diminishing human controllability. The aim of the paper is to discuss the future of the development of e-business in the era of the singularity by analyzing the business model transformation, management and decision-making, cybersecurity and sustainability, and competitiveness in global markets. The main outcome of the work will be that the sustainable development of e-business in the era of the singularity requires a new balance between algorithmic autonomy and human control, between technological efficiency and social responsibility.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Over the next decades, the nature of and possibilities for social connection will rapidly evolve with advances in artificial intelligence, mixed-reality technologies, and pervasive digital integration. Accordingly, psychological science must update how it conceptualizes and measures social connection. Here, we advance a three-part conceptual framework for understanding social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments. First, we situate social experiences within a dynamic relational ecosystem—a system of interaction partners and channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that together shape connection. Second, we conceptualize “alone” and “together” not as binary states but as a gradient shaped by level of physical copresence and communication (shades of aloneness and togetherness). Third, we conceptualize discrete social interactions as multidimensional, characterized by features such as interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition. Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades: the decoupling of objective and subjective connection, the erosion of “pure” solitude, the increasing effortfulness and value of in-person interaction, the fragmentation of shared reality, and the growing taken-for-grantedness of connection. We conclude by discussing methodological and applied implications of this framework.

Purpose This paper develops the concept of the human-machine symbioscape to explain how work environments shape collaboration between humans and AI-enabled machines. Extending servicescape thinking from customer-employee encounters to hybrid human-machine work systems, the paper positions environmental design as a core antecedent of human–machine adaptive collaboration, with particular relevance for service and frontline settings where visibility, coordination, and role clarity are critical. Design/methodology/approach The paper is conceptual and theory building in nature. It synthesises insights from biological symbiosis, servicescape research, sociotechnical and sociomaterial theory, organisational sensemaking and team adaptation research to develop a deductive typology of the human-machine symbioscape as a three-tiered environmental construct, its cue categories, and its design-critical properties. The framework is further illustrated through a structured coding of relevant human-machine collaboration studies. Findings The paper conceptualises the symbioscape as a three-tier environmental architecture comprising physical–digital, socio-relational, and institutional–ecosystem conditions. Across these tiers, six cue categories shape what human and AI-enabled actors can notice, how they coordinate work, and how collaborative routines are reinforced over time. Drawing on Weick's sensemaking theory, the framework links these tiers to enactment, selection, and retention processes, and explains how they influence adaptation speed, adaptation effectiveness, and adaptation persistence in human–AI collaboration. Research limitations/implications The paper is purely conceptual and does not empirically test the proposed relationships. Its evidence base is limited to published studies and illustrative coding, with a strong emphasis on service and frontline contexts. It identifies an agenda for future research around operationalising symbioscape constructs, testing the proposed relationships empirically, and examining how individual tiers and cross-tier configurations jointly affect human–machine work. Practical implications The symbioscape framework provides managers with a structured lens for designing AI-enabled workplaces. It highlights how deliberate choices in physical–digital visibility and interface design, socio-relational workflow sequencing and interaction load, and institutional governance, training, and role architecture can improve the speed, quality and durability of human–machine adaptation. The framework can be used to diagnose service work environments, where frontline employees must coordinate with intelligent systems under conditions of customer presence, temporal pressure, and operational variability. Originality/value The paper introduces the symbioscape as a novel, three-tier environmental construct for human–machine collaboration, extending the servicescape from customer–employee encounters to hybrid human–AI work systems. It adds a missing environmental layer to human-machine collaboration research by systematically integrating dispersed insights on context into a coherent framework that links environmental cue structures to sensemaking and adaptation outcomes. For scholars, it offers an integrative conceptual architecture; for practitioners, it provides a foundation for designing and structuring future workplaces that foster adaptive human–machine collaboration.

Brand-owned social media increasingly carries messages about enjoyment, participation, connection, purpose, and achievement, yet the same message may not produce the same response. This study examines how engagement-oriented brand content relates to comments and reposts across two brand contexts. Using PERMA as a semantic coding standard, we analyze 1,191 official Weibo posts from McDonald’s and Burberry in 2025. A Python-assisted LLM pipeline provides pre-annotation, followed by two-researcher reviews. OLS and PPML show a robust negative association between engagement-oriented content and reposting, while the comment association is less stable. Brand-specific results show greater heterogeneity for reposting. We define this as a narrow happiness backfire: content built around active involvement can be less portable across users’ networks even when it invites direct response. The findings show that conversation and public diffusion are distinct communication goals, so content designed to invite participation should not be assumed to travel widely.

This article examines the historical development of character education technologies, the pedagogical perspectives that have influenced their formation, and their potential for future advancement. It explores the traditions of folk pedagogy, the educational ideas of Eastern thinkers, and the distinctive characteristics of contemporary approaches to character education. Particular attention is given to the role of interactive methods, innovative pedagogical tools, and digital technologies in the educational process. The study emphasizes the importance of integrating national and universal human values, considering learners' individual characteristics, and developing independent thinking, social responsibility, and high moral standards. Furthermore, the article discusses the potential of artificial intelligence and modern technologies to enhance the effectiveness of character education in the future. Keywords: character education technologies, pedagogical heritage, development of character education, folk pedagogy, Eastern thinkers

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted in healthcare; however, the perceptions of undergraduate medical students in Nigeria on its role in clinical education remain underexplored. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI in clinical education across four public universities in Northeastern Nigeria. A mixed method cross-sectional survey was conducted between February and May, 2026 using a 27-items questionnaire. Convenience sampling approach was employed, and 200 valid responses were analysed. Likert data and free-text responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, respectively. Overall, 85.5% of the respondents reported a basic understanding of AI, 49.5% reported familiarity with AI in healthcare and 38.5% reported regular exposure to AI tools during their training. Most of the students perceived potential educational benefits: 90% agreed that AI could improve the quality of learning, and 85.5% agreed that it could enhance clinical decision support. However, 86% expressed concern that overreliance on AI could negatively affect clinical reasoning and judgement, while 59.5% believed AI could reduce hands-on practical training, and 57% agreed that it could replace medical roles. Only 20.5% of the respondent agreed to have adequate AI training in their medical curricula, while 72.5% supported incorporating AI into their curriculum. These findings suggest that respondents generally held positive perceptions of AI on clinical education but perceived some concerns about its responsible use and preparation for AI-enabled healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In contemporary education, the integration of artificial intelligence and gamification elements has become an important direction for enhancing students’ learning motivation and improving the teaching of complex subjects such as physics. However, the impact of artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology on the academic achievement of 7th-grade physics students has not yet been sufficiently explored in practical terms. Therefore, the aim of this study was to determine the effect of artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology on students’ academic achievement in 7th-grade physics and to substantiate its effectiveness scientifically. The study employed theoretical analysis of scientific and methodological literature, questionnaires, pedagogical observation, and practical work through interactive tasks, while the collected data were processed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. The results showed positive relationships among students’ interest in physics, understanding of the topic, acceptance of game elements, and perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence support, and it was also found that EducaPlay-based tasks and AI-assisted guidance increased classroom engagement. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the practical description of the effect of integrating artificial intelligence and gamification elements in 7th-grade physics and in clarifying its pedagogical potential. In conclusion, artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology can be considered an effective pedagogical tool for increasing interest in physics, strengthening learning activity, and improving students’ mastery of educational content in 7th-grade physics.

As automation progressively becomes integrated into decision-making environments, understanding why users fail to engage automated systems optimally remains crucial. The present study examined whether perceptions of time pressure could impact subjective and objective difficulty and its influence on use of discretionary automation. Seventy participants completed a visual search task under untimed and timed conditions, sometimes with the option to engage an automated aid. Results indicated that the time pressure increased both subjective and objective difficulty. Furthermore, participants used automation more frequently under the timed conditions. Despite the availability of a highly accurate system, participants did not engage the automation at rates to fully overcome the effects of time pressure. These findings suggest that users may turn to automation for support when task demands begin to increase, but these engagement decisions may not be driven to maximize performance outcomes.

Purpose. The purpose of the study was to demonstrate the effect of selected physiotherapy methods in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome treated conservatively and to verify whether a one-month structured therapeutic programme leads to a measurable improvement in pain, joint mobility and swelling of the hand. Materials and Methods. An observational study was carried out in a group of 8 adult patients (4 women, 4 men) aged 39–71 years (mean age 56.25 years) with grade 2 carpal tunnel syndrome. Each patient underwent an entry examination comprising history taking, anthropometric measurement of upper-limb circumferences in the area of the forearm, wrist and metacarpal heads, goniometric measurement of the active and passive mobility of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb in the sagittal and frontal planes using the SFTR method, and pain assessment on a numeric rating scale. The therapeutic programme lasted one month and consisted of 8 sessions of 50 minutes; it included kinesiotherapy, manual therapy, proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, stimulation of hand sensitivity, ultrasound applied to the palmar aspect of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb (3 MHz, 50 Hz, pulse-pause ratio 1:2, intensity 1.0–1.6 W·cm⁻²) and kinesiology taping. Input and output values were compared using the one-tailed paired t-test at a level of significance α = 0.05. Results. The range of motion of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb increased in both planes, for the active (sagittal plane p = 0.0001917; frontal plane p = 0.000005688) as well as for the passive range of motion (p = 0.00291 and p = 0.00002326). The intensity of pain decreased from a mean value of 4 to 2.625 (p = 0.00006782). The circumferences decreased in the area of the wrist (p = 0.01047) and of the metacarpal heads (p = 0.04749), while the forearm circumference remained unchanged. Conclusions. One month of targeted physiotherapy significantly reduced pain and swelling and improved the mobility of the thumb in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome. Conservative physiotherapeutic management combined with education in the principles of ergonomics can be recommended before considering surgical decompression in patients with a mild and moderate form of the syndrome.

Crew performance determines the safety and operational efficiency of shipping companies, yet human factors remain the dominant cause of maritime accidents. This study aims to analyze the influence of English language competence, digital literacy, grit, and technostress on crew performance, with human capital capability serving as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed, utilizing a survey of 316 seafarers from shipping companies in Indonesia, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS. The results indicate that: 1) English language competence has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 2) Digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 3) Grit has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 4) Technostress does not have a significant effect on human capital capability; 5) English language competence does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 6) Digital literacy does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 7) Grit has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 8) Technostress does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 9) Human capital capability has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 10) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of English language competence on crew performance; 11) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of digital literacy on crew performance; 12) Human capital capability partially mediates the effect of grit on crew performance; 13) Human capital capability does not mediate the effect of technostress on crew performance. Shipping companies need to enhance crew performance by strengthening human capital capability through maritime English training, digital literacy development, and mental resilience building. The novelty of this study lies in examining human capital capability as a mediating mechanism among Indonesian seafarers.

ENGLISH This critical essay examines the knowledge that may be lost when technological innovation is described only through its visible outcome. Drawing on work on invisible labour, articulation work, design rationale, knowledge boundaries and organizational learning, it distinguishes the context-dependent rejection of an alternative from evidence of its general infeasibility. The paper proposes a six-field record for preserving actual alternatives considered, criteria, gaps in evidence, responsible decisions and conditions for reconsideration. A hypothetical photopolymer case illustrates the difference between a selected option, an option rejected under defined constraints and an option left unresolved by insufficient evidence. The proposed record has not been empirically validated, does not claim methodological priority, and is explicitly distinguished from the author's earlier technical publications. Version 1. English and Spanish editions deposited together. ESPAÑOL Este ensayo crítico examina el conocimiento que puede perderse cuando una innovación tecnológica se describe únicamente por su resultado visible. A partir de antecedentes sobre trabajo invisible, trabajo de articulación, justificación de decisiones de diseño, fronteras del conocimiento y aprendizaje organizativo, distingue el descarte de una alternativa en un contexto determinado de la prueba de su inviabilidad general. Propone una ficha de seis campos para conservar las alternativas realmente consideradas, los criterios aplicados, las lagunas de evidencia, las decisiones y sus responsables, así como las condiciones que justificarían reconsiderarlas. Un ejemplo hipotético con materiales fotopolimerizables ilustra la distinción entre una opción seleccionada, otra descartada bajo restricciones definidas y una tercera sin evidencia suficiente. La ficha no se ha validado empíricamente, no reivindica prioridad metodológica y se diferencia expresamente de publicaciones técnicas anteriores del autor. Versión 1. Ediciones inglesa y española depositadas juntas.

This research outline sets out the proposed argument, derivations, evidence requirements and limitations for “The Mandate as a Unit of Risk.” The proposed paper connects the authority under which an AI agent acts with the economics of task reliability, oversight and adverse outcomes. It treats the mandate as a versioned authority for a class of acts, enforced through a permission that can be refused before an act is executed. The research programme examines how a mandate can express an admissible set of model-and-oversight configurations and a quantitative risk appetite, with authority narrowing automatically on independently adjudicated evidence and widening only with an authorised human signature. It extends the task-value framework with the cost of refusal and escalation, examines calibration in financial services, and identifies the conditions and limitations of any proposed assurance statement. The outline distinguishes established precedents from candidate contributions and identifies simulation and empirical work still required. Publication status: This deposit is a research outline, not a completed or peer-reviewed paper. Proposed theoretical results, calibration procedures and empirical tests remain to be established. Cordier’s simulation layer has not been independently rerun; the outline states the assumptions on which its proposed analysis depends.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of job insecurity in the relationships between technology threat perception, artificial intelligence anxiety, and organizational commitment. Data were collected from 387 full-time employees across multiple sectors in Türkiye through a cross-sectional survey. The hypothesized model was tested using structural equation modeling (AMOS 24), following confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrap-based mediation analysis (5,000 resamples). Technology threat perception and AI anxiety were both positively associated with job insecurity, which in turn was negatively associated with organizational commitment. Both stressors also showed significant direct negative associations with organizational commitment, and bootstrap analysis confirmed significant indirect effects through job insecurity, indicating complementary partial mediation. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is among the first studies to jointly model technology threat perception and AI anxiety as co-occurring antecedents of job insecurity within a single structural framework linking both to organizational commitment, extending cognitive stress appraisal theory, Conservation of Resources theory, and Social Exchange Theory to the context of AI-driven workplace change, with region-specific evidence from Türkiye.

The management of mitral valve disease is rapidly evolving, driven by advances in multimodality imaging, surgical techniques, transcatheter therapies, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this changing landscape, the traditional Heart Team model should evolve toward a more integrated and dynamic multidisciplinary approach. The “Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0” may combine detailed anatomical and functional characterization with surgical expertise, transcatheter treatment options, and AI-assisted data integration to support individualized treatment strategies. Advanced imaging increasingly informs not only diagnosis but also procedural planning and patient selection, while AI may improve reproducibility of mitral regurgitation assessment, risk stratification, and phenotypic characterization. However, these technologies should augment rather than replace expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making. This Communication discusses the emerging components of this paradigm and proposes a practical framework in which imaging specialists, surgeons, interventional cardiologists, heart failure specialists, and data-driven tools interact throughout the patient pathway. The objective is not to create a larger Heart Team, but a more integrated one, capable of matching the right patient to the right treatment at the right time.

The Observer-Relative Interpretation Problem & The I or O Test™ presents an evolving philosophical framework examining the relationship between observation, interpretation, identity, love, self-preservation, and continuity. The original working paper, developed October 23, 2026, investigates how different observers may encounter the same information yet arrive at different interpretations. It distinguishes physical and chemical information from meta-interpretation, proposing that the observer's perspective influences understanding without necessarily changing the underlying reality. An experimental appendix, developed October 28, 2026, introduces The I or O Test™, a proposed six-photograph observation exercise followed by personal explanation, a provisional trial period, and consideration of traceable behavioral evidence. The experiment introduces three observer-relative outcomes: I: Passed with insufficient evidence. O: Failed the experiment's stated criteria. i: The observed individual provided an explanation that convinced the observer. The appendix further develops the Birth Star Principle™, proposing that individuals differ in what they regard as essential to their self-preservation. Additional symbolic concepts include Pearly's Continuation, the collaboration of O and I through love, and the emergence of Newi. The central philosophical proposition is that observation does not confer complete knowledge of another individual. Interpretation remains provisional, and the observer must remain willing to correct their own understanding. This publication is an original, exploratory philosophical proposal. Its symbolic terminology and experimental classifications are not scientifically validated psychological assessments, diagnostic categories, or established physical laws. Author: Elyse Meagan Estes Editorial assistance: Q (ChatGPT, OpenAI), AI-assisted organization, drafting, and methodological clarification. Research status: Independent conceptual research; not peer-reviewed.

This practical guide, prepared by the Student Scientific Society of the Presidential Academy (RANEPA), supports students taking their first steps in research. It is structured as a journey map of eight stages: understanding science, finding sources, conducting research, writing, publishing, presenting, growing and getting support, and being part of the academic community. The guide explains how scientific knowledge differs from opinion, how academic degrees, titles and positions are organized, and how science is governed and funded in Russia. It covers systematic literature search, including eLIBRARY, CyberLeninka and the RANEPA library. It also covers research design (problem, object, subject, aim, objectives, hypothesis and methods) and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in line with the Academy’s Academic Integrity and AI Policy. Further sections address academic writing and the IMRAD structure, citation styles, plagiarism and originality, and choosing journals indexed in RSCI or listed by the Higher Attestation Commission and the Unified State List of Scientific Journals. They also explain how to recognize predatory publications, the peer-review process, and preparing conference presentations. Finally, the guide describes scholarships, grants, the student research portfolio and the structure of the Student Scientific Society. Each section includes step-by-step instructions, screenshots, QR codes to official resources and practical tips. A glossary of key terms is included. Keywords: young researcher, student research, academic writing, research design, scientific publishing, academic integrity, student scientific society, RANEPA

This chapter explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is influencing reflective practice in second language teacher education, along with the discussion on ethics and the developmental implications of AI-powered reflection. It conceptualizes AI-powered reflection as a form of technological mediation that alters how teaching experience is externalized and interpreted through algorithmic processes. Grounding in distributed cognition, this chapter positions AI as a cognitive artifact that shapes reflective activity while teacher professional meaning-making and accountability remains situated in teachers’ judgment. It shows how the influence of algorithmic mediation on reflective authority, agency and temporal depth has specific implications for professional novice teachers. Ethical considerations are presented as fundamental to the responsible integration of AI-powered reflective tools. The chapter further introduces a human-centered framework to inform their design and pedagogical use in teacher education and identifies future directions for research and practice that seek to sustain reflective depth and teacher agency within mentoring relationships and professional learning contexts. It concludes that AI can enhance reflective support when its use is guided by ethical commitments and remains aligned with the developmental purposes of professional development.

We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.

Work productivity reflects the extent to which workers are able to carry out their responsibilities effectively during the production process. Workers’ eating patterns, including whether they consume breakfast before starting their activities, may be relevant to their physical readiness and ability to perform their tasks. This study examined the association between breakfast habits and work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia in 2026. A quantitative observational study using a cross-sectional design was carried out among 120 production department workers, from whom 55 respondents were included as the study sample. Information regarding breakfast habits and work productivity was obtained through questionnaires. The collected data were subsequently analyzed using the Chi-Square test with Continuity Correction. Among the 55 respondents, 40 workers (72.7%) reported that they did not have a regular breakfast habit, whereas 15 workers (27.3%) reported having a breakfast habit. Regarding productivity, 37 respondents (67.3%) were categorized as having low work productivity, while 18 respondents (32.7%) were categorized as having high productivity. Statistical analysis produced a p-value of 0.003 (p < 0.05), demonstrating a significant association between breakfast habits and work productivity. The proportion of workers with high productivity was greater among those who reported having breakfast than among those who did not. The study concludes that breakfast habits are significantly associated with work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia. These findings support the consideration of healthy breakfast practices as part of occupational health promotion and efforts to encourage adequate nutritional intake among workers

Purpose Knowledge work is extensively location-independent, making flexible work designs more common. However, organizations foster various practices regarding the level of autonomy and control, affecting employee well-being and productivity. To support strategic and operative work design, this paper aims to explain the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity, considering the mediating role of managerial culture. Design/methodology/approach This paper describes a quantitative survey featuring 1,057 respondents. It tests with a regression analysis a hypothesized model, in which the level of individual work autonomy, mediated by managerial culture, predicts well-being and productivity. Findings The analysis indicated that decision-making autonomy has a direct positive relationship with productivity. Furthermore, autonomy in working practices has a direct positive relationship with both well-being and productivity. Managerial culture mediates the relationship between decision-making autonomy and both outcome variables. Originality/value This paper provides empirical evidence of the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity. The academic value of this paper lies in the multiple dimensions of autonomy it addresses, yielding novel data on the outcomes in a comparative manner. As a pragmatic contribution, it provides input to managerial culture design.

This study examines the relationships between artificial intelligence-induced job insecurity, affective commitment, job performance, and turnover intention, with particular attention to the mediating roles of affective commitment and job performance. The analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling to assess the direct and indirect relationships among the variables. Data were collected from 400 employees working in different sectors through online and face-to-face surveys using a convenience sampling method. The findings indicate that AI-induced job insecurity is positively associated with turnover intention and negatively associated with affective commitment, whereas its direct association with job performance is not statistically significant. Affective commitment is positively associated with job performance and negatively associated with turnover intention. The mediation analyses indicate that affective commitment significantly mediates the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention and between AI-induced job insecurity and job performance. In contrast, the mediating role of job performance in the relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention is not supported. Overall, the findings suggest that affective commitment represents an important explanatory pathway in the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and employees’ work-related outcomes.

This study aims to analyze the influence of Language Literacy on Academic Writing Ability with Artificial Intelligence as a mediating variable in Ambon State Polytechnic students. Academic writing ability is one of the important competencies that students must have in producing quality scientific work. However, the development of Artificial Intelligence technology has changed the learning patterns and academic writing processes of students. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. The study population was Ambon State Polytechnic students, with a sample of 50 respondents determined using a purposive sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) based on Partial Least Square (PLS) with the help of SmartPLS 4. The results of the study indicate that Language Literacy has a positive and significant effect on Artificial Intelligence, Artificial Intelligence has a positive and significant effect on Academic Writing Ability, while Language Literacy has a positive but insignificant effect on Academic Writing Ability. In addition, Artificial Intelligence is proven to significantly mediate the relationship between Language Literacy and Academic Writing Ability. The results of the study indicate that Artificial Intelligence acts as a full mediator in this relationship. This finding indicates that the improvement of students' academic writing ability is not only determined by language literacy skills, but also by the ability to utilize Artificial Intelligence effectively in the learning process and academic writing.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has renewed debates on the nature of creativity. This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in the development of creativity skills among middle school teachers and students through comparative perspectives. Using a qualitative case study design, the research involved 87 participants—42 teachers from different subject areas and 45 eighth-grade students—from public middle schools in Bursa, Turkey, during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed via content analysis. The findings reveal that AI plays a dual role in the creative process: it facilitates idea generation and imagination, yet may restrict originality when used without pedagogical guidance. While students tend to view artificial intelligence as a tool that accelerates production, teachers emphasize risks such as cognitive offloading and superficial learning. Artificial intelligence becomes an effective educational tool only when embedded within ethically grounded, teacher-guided, and AI literacy–oriented frameworks. Subject-based analyses show that, particularly in Science and Mathematics, teachers position AI as a supportive cognitive partner that facilitates visualization and conceptual understanding, yet caution that unguided use may replace deep learning with surface-level content production.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Smart-school projects increasingly combine sensors, dashboards and artificial intelligence, but their managerial value remains weak when attendance, access control, energy use and reporting operate as isolated modules. This paper proposes a Smart School Management System (SSMS) in which Internet-of-Things observations are transformed into auditable decisions through a policy-constrained multi-agent architecture. Unlike component-level smart-campus prototypes, the contribution is an orchestration model linking perception agents, decision agents and a coordination agent under privacy, traceability and human-oversight constraints. The empirical part uses the open UCI Occupancy Detection dataset (20,560 labelled records) to validate the perception layer on a reproducible occupancy-classification task. Trained on 8,143 records and tested on 12,417 records, logistic regression achieved 98.34% accuracy and 0.9659 F1-score, outperforming a simple light-threshold rule (94.36% accuracy, 0.8961 F1). These results validate only the occupancy-perception component under the stated open-data protocol; they do not validate the complete smart-school system or institutional deployment. The paper therefore advances a reproducible, ethically governed and practically deployable direction for autonomous educational management.

Digital transformation changes the conditions under which organizations produce and use knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds new ways to search, predict, generate, and evaluate information. Yet greater use of these tools does not establish that research becomes more reliable or more original. This paper develops a critical narrative review and descriptive secondary-data analysis to examine that distinction. Selected publications on organizational change, AI-assisted work, scientific discovery, and governance provide the conceptual foundation. Published statistics from Stanford's AI Index and Eurostat illustrate changes in adoption between 2023 and 2025. The two series are analysed separately because their populations and measurement procedures differ. The evidence indicates expanding use, but adoption statistics cannot demonstrate causal improvements in research quality. An original conceptual framework links digital foundations and AI capabilities with changes in research practice, conditioned by human expertise, institutional arrangements, and governance. Four propositions translate the framework into questions for future testing. The proposed agenda prioritizes reproducibility, task-specific evaluation, skill development, equitable participation, and preservation of intellectual diversity. The paper concludes that future research should evaluate the complete knowledge-production process, including verification and correction costs, rather than treating faster output as sufficient evidence of progress. No primary survey, experiment, or model validation is claimed. The contribution is an integrated account of how organizations can study AI-enabled transformation while maintaining the evidentiary standards needed for credible knowledge
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ObjectiveThree digital ranked choice voting ballots were investigated to assess the impact of formatting on usability.BackgroundRanked choice voting (RCV) is a ballot format that allows voters to rank candidate choices in order of preference. The design of the ballot has a notable impact on usability, and this remains a challenge for RCV.MethodThis experiment investigated the usability of three RCV electronic ballot formats (bubble grid, column, and hand-numbered). Completion times, errors, subjective usability ratings, and trust data were collected.ResultsThe three formats took subjects 50-70 seconds on average to vote for a single contest. The ballots also had high error rates, which ranged from 23-38%. The hand-numbered format had the worst performance, as it had the highest completion times, error rates, and the lowest subjective usability ratings.ConclusionThis research highlights usability issues with RCV digital ballots. The formats tested were inefficient and ineffective, and performed poorly in comparison to previously tested plurality digital ballots.ApplicationThis experiment raises concerns about the scalability of RCV to larger elections. Ballots with RCV take longer to vote on and have higher error rates, which should be taken into consideration by election administrators.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping second language (L2) writing by introducing new forms of interaction between learners and intelligent technologies. This conceptual paper examines the potential opportunities and critical challenges of GenAI in L2 writing, drawing on a purposively selected body of recent scholarship. It suggests that GenAI can provide contingent support throughout the writing process, facilitate idea generation and revision, and expand opportunities for multilingual composing through L1-mediated and translanguaging practices. At the same time, excessive reliance on AI may lead to cognitive offloading and weaken learners’ engagement in higher-order writing processes. Concerns about inaccurate information and fabricated citations further highlight the need for independent verification and critical AI literacy. Moreover, unequal access to technological resources, AI literacy, and educational support may contribute to an emerging AI divide and reproduce existing educational and linguistic inequalities. The paper argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends on how it is integrated into learners’ writing processes and on whether it supports sustained engagement, learner agency, and reflective thinking and decision-making without displacing their intellectual and authorial responsibilities.

Can an agent be in contact with all other agents without being dissolved in them? We give this question a precise topological form. A pairwise-contact foam is a family of regions ("bubbles") of a state space with pairwise disjoint interiors, which represent the preserved individuality of each agent, such that every two regions touch, which represents connection, ideally along a set of positive size. We show that the naive formulation of the condition is degenerate unless the regions are regular closed with nonempty interior, and that point contact is cheap in dimension \( \ge2 \) while contact along arcs is impossible in the plane for more than four disks. We then prove that foams exist for every number \( N\ge2 \) of regions and, in the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \( \ell^2 \), for countably infinitely many regions covering the whole space: the regions \( D_k=\{x:|x_k|\ge|x_j|\ \forall j\} \) meet pairwise along codimension-one walls \( x_k=\pm x_l \). In dimension three and on orientable surfaces of higher genus the planar obstruction is bypassed as well. Gluing along contact sets leaves every piece intact, which is the formal sense of "union without dissolution". Pairwise contact is strictly weaker than the Wada property, and riddled basins are a degenerate, non-proper case. For empirical use we separate three quantities that are easily confused: the global separation \( d(C_i,C_j) \) of two regions, the switching distance \( d(x,C_j) \) from a given state, and the activation distance to the contact set, together with intervention-specific versions that depend on an actuation model. We replace a single adjacency density by the spectrum of separations, a threshold-free completion scale, and a persistent nerve, with explicit limits on what the nerve proves, dimension-aware null models, and a rule that unsupported regions make a test inconclusive rather than being deleted. We define preservation of an agent's own control pattern so that it includes distinguishability of agents, give a confirmatory test of the composite hypothesis H4 whose unit of analysis is the independent replicate, and outline falsifiable programs in morphospace navigation by bioelectric interventions and in the information topology of human, AI, and biological collectives, including prediction of group fragmentation. No empirical result is claimed. The interpretive layer (cognitive light cone, "noosphere") is kept strictly apart from the mathematical and testable layers.

This paper studies text documents for natural language processing using toolsfrom dynamical systems and topological data analysis. We model a document’sparagraph procession as a discrete semantic trajectory moving around a centralthematic limit cycle Γ in a high-dimensional vocabulary space. Following Majhi,we prove that the Vietoris-Rips homology of the paragraph point cloud near Γ isisomorphic to either 0 or Z under precise density and reach constraints. We also providea geometric proof using the Tubular Neighborhood Theorem, the Borsuk NerveTheorem, and Latschev’s Reconstruction Theorem. The uniform and non-uniformconvergences of a text’s paragraphs to its main theme are rigorously establishedusing Oseledet’s Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem and Pesin’s metric construction.Furthermore, we derive the exponential convergence of the time-evolved persistencediagrams to the geometric profile of Γ via the results on Bottleneck distance for twodistinct temporal-shifted configurations. Finally, we demonstrate that non-essentialwritings and creative noise within a text systematically compress into the dead diagonalsubstrate using 0-persistence exponent formulations. With our results, welist some properties and term a text with these properties as a well-written text.Conversely, any text lacking one or more of these properties may be classified aspoorly written. Generative AI agents can utilize these constraints to automaticallyimprove their own writing quality and objectively evaluate human text.

This chapter outlines the personal and professional foundations of the cognitive behavioural approach developed for occupational health practice. Both occupational health and cognitive behavioural therapy became a vocation for me, providing a stabilising and meaningful thread that supported my movement beyond personal adversity and shaped my progression from nursing into trauma therapy and expert-witness work. The chapter traces a 40-year professional journey alongside the evolution of occupational health, from its earlier focus on industrial injury to its current role as a clinically grounded specialty. It considers how changes in the nature of work, together with increasing recognition of psychological and social influences on health, have reshaped contemporary occupational health practice. My thinking has been strongly influenced by the work of Gordon Waddell, Tom Cox, Cary Cooper and others whose research laid the foundations for biopsychosocial and psychologically informed approaches to work and health. These influences supported my development as both an occupational health practitioner and cognitive behavioural therapist and continue to guide my clinical reasoning. This chapter therefore introduces the values, evidence base and reasoning that underpin the cognitive behavioural approach explored throughout this book.

The growing demand for intelligent and adaptive services is accelerating the transition from conventional communication systems to semantic communication. Task-Oriented Semantic Communication (ToSC) has emerged as an efficient framework that reduces communication cost by transmitting only task-relevant information for downstream processing. This survey reviews the theoretical foundations, system architectures, and enabling technologies of ToSC, providing a taxonomy of design strategies spanning collaborative edge inference, end-to-end optimization, and multi-agent cooperation. Key technologies, including deep learning-based semantic representation and adaptive joint source-channel coding, are discussed. Device heterogeneity and partial observability are examined alongside recent tasks' performance evaluations, such as classification and recognition. The survey also discusses the integration of large-scale multimodal foundation models into semantic encoders for zero-shot task adaptation, continual learning frameworks for on-device semantic processing, cooperative multi-agent reasoning with interpretable information exchange, and cross-layer co-design within AI-native 6G infrastructures, leveraging reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and digital twins. By consolidating existing knowledge and identifying key design trade-offs in latency, accuracy, and bandwidth efficiency, this work aims to serve as both a reference and a roadmap for advancing ToSC toward reliable and resource-efficient communication in 6G and beyond.

As enterprise organizations transition from single-turn large language model (LLM) assistants to autonomous multi-agent execution meshes speaking the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, traditional perimeter-based access controls fail to prevent confused-deputy privilege escalation, batch-array policy bypass, and non-repudiable audit gaps. Building directly upon the foundational Zero Trust Architecture principles established in Durga (2025, DOI: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i12.1050) and the multi-agent coordination taxonomies formalized in Durga (2025, DOIs: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i11.1049, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i10.1048, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i9.1047, and 10.5281/zenodo.23723284), this technical report specifies and benchmarks three production enforcement invariants implemented across the OWASP Agent Control Standard (ACS) and the AgentTrust open specification: (1) per-element JSON-RPC 2.0 batch decomposition with deterministic fail-closed semantics; (2) cryptographic monotonic capability attenuation across transitive delegation hops; and (3) RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) audit receipts mapped to Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF v1.3.0) provenance records.

Deploying autonomous AI agents across discrete and process manufacturing environments introduces acute cyber-physical risks when enterprise cloud control planes interact with plant-floor systems across ERP, MES, WMS, and QMS. Extending the self-optimizing factory paradigm formulated in Durga (2025, DOI: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i8.1046) and the cloud-native platform architectures established in Durga (2025, DOIs: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i7.1045, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i6.1044, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i5.1043, and 10.5281/zenodo.23723284), this technical report presents deterministic benchmarks for governed industrial agent operations and edge AI model fleets. We evaluate a 4-mode Pre-Release Recovery Reservation Lease with compare-and-swap (CAS) fencing, a cycle-safe transitive rollback DAG across ISA-95 Level 3/4 systems, a hard physical safety firewall isolating Level 0/1 Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS), and a Two-Layer JCS/CBOR Merkle edge model custody protocol achieving sub-100 ms last-known-good (LKG) rollback under intermittent plant connectivity.

A dated test protocol, not a pre-registration, for a study of Estonia's policy on identifiers for artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The study traces the move from an agent identifier discussed in June 2026 as an isikukood (the Estonian personal identification code) to a design that keeps the agent from being a person, and the draft act that the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) sent for inter-ministerial coordination on 08.10.2026 (draft legislation information system, EIS, file 26-1105). It uses explaining-outcome process tracing on its theory-first path. The protocol sets out the rival explanations, the observables that bear on them and how each is tested, the coding design with a human second coder, the collection rules, and the author's interventions in the process, each with its date. documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from pilot programs into the routine delivery of military mental health care. Predictive models already scan Veterans Health Administration records to flag veterans at high risk of suicide; models trained on Army Study to Assess Risk and Resilience in Servicemembers data can now stratify suicide risk up to a decade after soldiers leave active service, and generative AI models are being positioned to deliver triage, peer support, and low-intensity psychological interventions. The frameworks that govern responsible military AI have not kept up. The Department of Defense Responsible Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Pathway, NATO’s principles of responsible use, and allied instruments such as the United Kingdom’s JSP 936 provide lifecycle assurance for AI-enabled capability, but none of them makes specific provision for the therapeutic encounter. That omission exposes service members to what this commentary terms a recognition-action gap. Systems trained predominantly on civilian data can transcribe the words of military distress accurately while misreading their clinical meaning: moral injury classified as fear-based trauma, minimized suicidality scored as low risk, routine operational vernacular flagged as threat. The risk is compounded because the boundary between clinical care and occupational capability is porous in the armed forces. The military command exception to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act Privacy Rule and command notification under Department of Defense Instruction 6490.08 mean that outputs generated for care could lawfully reach deployability, security clearance, and administrative decisions, with predictable consequences for help-seeking. This commentary proposes behavioral validity, the demonstrated capability to safely manage the behavioral presentations of the population a system will actually serve, as a core governance requirement for mental health AI in defense settings. It specifies 4 conditions of use: clinically supervised pre-fielding assessment, therapeutic firewalling, moral injury and cultural competency, and meaningful human control. Defense health systems should not wait for civilian regulators to notice the gap. They are well placed to define the standard.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now drafts travel itineraries that travelers cannot easily verify. Integrating privacy calculus theory with a dual-pathway trust model, this study examines how system attributes shape tourist trust and continued usage, and how technology readiness conditions those links. A two-wave panel (433 Chinese and European travelers), a validation wave (372), and 42 interviews were analyzed using structural equation modeling, importance–performance map analysis, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and thematic analysis. Data transparency and content authenticity raised both cognitive and affective trust, and affective trust sustained continued usage most strongly. Technology readiness reversed the expected pattern: readier travelers scrutinized fluent output rather than relying on it, weakening the behavioral effect of trust. Providers should replace generic privacy notices with in-context, verifiable data-use disclosures and checkable citations, and segment interfaces so that ready travelers receive verification tools and less-ready travelers receive reassurance. Regulators can make verifiability, not fluency, the disclosure standard.

Background/Objectives: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are entering clinical documentation ahead of institutional governance, and little is known about whether clinicians who rely on them also check their output, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe. This study characterized regular GenAI use for documentation, verification practices, and exposure to clinically relevant errors among healthcare professionals at a Romanian tertiary center, and identified the attitudes independently associated with regular use. Methods: In a cross-sectional survey of 126 physicians, residents, nurses, and public health specialists (46.0% of 315 invited), regular use was defined as at least weekly use for documentation during the preceding three months. Composites measured AI literacy, trust in output accuracy, perceived confidentiality risk, perceived usefulness, documentation burden, and intention; emotional exhaustion was measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory. Correlates of regular use were examined with bootstrap-validated multivariable logistic regression, and differences in burden and exhaustion with propensity-score overlap weighting. Results: Regular use was reported by 56 participants (44.4%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 36.1–53.2), mostly with ChatGPT (89.3%) for referral and discharge letters (78.6%) and discharge summaries (69.6%). Users verified a mean of 70.3% (95% CI 65.6–75.0) of outputs line by line, and 36 (64.3%; 95% CI 51.2–75.5) had encountered at least one clinically relevant error. Among users, higher trust was associated with a lower proportion of outputs verified (Spearman ρ = −0.31; p = 0.020). Concern about factual errors was common in both groups (73.2% vs. 77.1%), whereas confidentiality concern, perceived insufficient training, and fear of liability were less frequent among users. Higher trust (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.36 per 10 points; 95% CI 1.34–4.15), higher perceived usefulness (OR 1.90; 1.03–3.50), and lower perceived risk (OR 0.49; 0.29–0.83) were independently associated with regular use (optimism-corrected area under the curve 0.905). After overlap weighting, differences in documentation burden (−4.8 points; 95% CI −12.1 to 2.6) and emotional exhaustion (−1.7; −5.9 to 2.5) were not statistically significant but were imprecisely estimated. Conclusions: Regular GenAI use coexisted with incomplete verification and frequent error exposure and was linked to trust and perceived usefulness; AI literacy and training were not independently associated with use once these attitudes were accounted for. Associations with documentation burden and emotional exhaustion were inconclusive. Institutions should treat verification as a distinct, trainable behavior and pair access with explicit confidentiality guidance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in health care and is increasingly being explored in hospital pharmacy practice. Hospital pharmacists manage large amounts of medication-related information, including prescriptions, patient medical records, laboratory values, drug interactions, adverse drug reactions, medication histories and inventory data. AI-based technologies can analyse these data rapidly and may assist pharmacists in identifying medication-related problems, improving workflow and supporting clinical decision-making. Recent literature describes applications of AI in prescription screening, medication-error detection, adverse drug event detection, pharmacovigilance, medication reconciliation, dose optimization, clinical decision support, antimicrobial stewardship, inventory management and medication adherence Machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing are among the major technologies used in pharmacy-related AI applications. These technologies can identify patterns in electronic health records and clinical documentation that may be difficult to recognize manually. However, AI should be considered a support tool rather than a complete replacement for pharmacists. Concerns related to data quality, privacy algorithmic bias, explainability, cybersquatting, cost training and clinical validation remain important. Successful implementation therefore requires collaboration between pharmacists, physicians, information technology professionals, hospital administrators and AI developers. The review discusses the major applications, advantages, limitations, ethical considerations and future perspectives of AI in hospital pharmacy practice.

documents.abstract: This study qualitatively inquired into artificial intelligence and the future of audit in Nigeria, specifically investigating whether AI will replace the human auditor. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-eight (28) participants were purposively selected across Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt, comprising Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, audit managers/seniors with 10+ years of experience, ICAN/ANAN/FRCN regulators, and audited clients including CFOs and Audit Committee chairs. Data were collected via semi-structured indepth interviews between January and May 2025. Data saturation was achieved at the 23rd interview. Thematic analysis was performed using the Braun and Clarke (2006) framework assisted by NVivo. Results reveal that AI is augmenting, not replacing, human auditors. Four distinct AI implementation levels emerged: Assisted Audit (e.g., IDEA, Excel), Augmented Audit (e.g., Power BI, ACL), Autonomous Testing (e.g., RPA, Machine Learning anomaly detection), and Advisory Assurance (e.g., Generative AI for reporting). AI deployment improved audit efficiency by 60% and increased anomaly detection from 35% to 82%. Key barriers to adoption include technophobia (78%), unstructured client data (72%), tool costs (65%), and a regulatory vacuum regarding AI audit evidence under ISA 500 (60%). The study proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Model (70-30 Model), where AI performs 70% of routine data tasks, and human auditors provide 30% high-level professional judgement, ethics, and skepticism. This represents the first phenomenological study in Nigeria exploring the lived experiences of senior practitioners on the AI replacement debate.

ObjectiveTo describe the experience of pain among people with Parkinson's disease, including its characteristics, psychological effects, and impact on daily life.DesignQualitative descriptive study.SettingCommunity-based study using semi-structured individual interviews.ParticipantsFifteen people with Parkinson's disease (11 women) diagnosed according to the United Kingdom Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria and experiencing Parkinson's disease-related pain based on the Parkinson's Disease Pain Classification System.InterventionNot applicable.Main measuresSemi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' experiences of pain. Data were analysed using an inductive thematic analysis based on a hybrid approach combining artificial intelligence-powered coding through ChatGPT-4 with manual triangulation.ResultsThree main themes were identified: (1) experiences and perceptions of pain, including the nature and characterization of pain and its relationship with Parkinson's disease; (2) the impact of pain on daily life; and (3) feelings associated with pain, including emotional changes related to pain and its broader psychological impact.ConclusionsPain in people with Parkinson's disease is an interconnected and context-dependent experience extending beyond its physical manifestations. The patient-centred narratives provide contextual insight into how pain interacts with motor and non-motor symptoms, daily functioning, emotional well-being, and participation, supporting individualized and comprehensive approaches to pain assessment and management.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Objective: The paper aimed to examine ethical, privacy, and governance challenges in AI-IoT (Artificial Intelligence-based Internet of Things) healthcare environments. Design: A total of 39 peer-reviewed open-access studies were screened and used for a systematic review using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework. A multi-stage thematic analysis was used for identifying recurring patterns within the literature and answering the research questions. Results/outcomes: The identified challenges in the AI-IoT healthcare ecosystems, arising from the thematic analysis, are privacy and continuous surveillance, algorithmic bias and lack of explainability, limitations for informed consent, and fragmented governance and accountability. Conclusion: The findings, in sync with STS theory, indicate that challenges in AI-IoT healthcare systems cannot be addressed solely through technological innovations. In response, the study proposed an Integrated Human-Centric Trust Framework to integrate human intervention with technological advancements.
